statement: Liver cancer is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the liver.
source_span: Liver cancer is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the liver.

statement: The liver has four lobes and fills the upper right side of the abdomen inside the rib cage.
source_span: It has four lobes and fills the upper right side of the abdomen inside the rib cage.

statement: Liver cancer is the fourth most common cancer and the third leading cause of cancer death in the world.
source_span: Liver cancer is the fourth most common cancer and the third leading cause of cancer death in the world.

statement: In the United States, men—especially Asian/Pacific Islander men—have an increased risk of liver cancer.
source_span: men, especially Asian/Pacific Islander men, have an increased risk of liver cancer

statement: People are usually older than 40 years when they develop liver cancer.
source_span: People are usually older than 40 years when they develop this cancer.

statement: There are six types of the hepatitis virus, and hepatitis A, B, and C are the three most common types.
source_span: There are six types of the hepatitis virus. Hepatitis A (HAV), hepatitis B (HBV), and hepatitis C (HCV) are the three most common types.

statement: There is no vaccine to prevent infection with hepatitis C, though vaccines exist for hepatitis A and hepatitis B.
source_span: The Hepatitis A vaccine and the hepatitis B vaccine prevent infection with hepatitis A and hepatitis B. There is no vaccine to prevent infection with hepatitis C.

statement: Hepatitis D develops only in people already infected with hepatitis B.
source_span: Hepatitis D develops in people already infected with hepatitis B.

statement: Being infected with hepatitis G virus (HGV) has not been shown to cause liver cancer.
source_span: Being infected with hepatitis G virus (HGV) has not been shown to cause liver cancer.

statement: Risk factors for liver cancer include hepatitis B and C, cirrhosis, and aflatoxin, while the hepatitis B vaccine is a protective factor.
source_span: The following risk factors may increase the risk of liver cancer: - Hepatitis B and C - Cirrhosis - Aflatoxin ... The following protective factor may decrease the risk of liver cancer: - Hepatitis B vaccine

statement: The risk of liver cancer is even greater for people with both hepatitis B and C, and risk increases the longer the hepatitis infection lasts, especially hepatitis C.
source_span: The risk is even greater for people with both hepatitis B and C. Also, the longer the hepatitis infection lasts (especially hepatitis C), the greater the risk.

statement: Chronic alcoholism and chronic hepatitis C are the most common causes of cirrhosis.
source_span: Chronic alcoholism and chronic hepatitis C are the most common causes of cirrhosis.

statement: Aflatoxin is a poison from a fungus that can grow on improperly stored foods such as grains and nuts.
source_span: aflatoxin (poison from a fungus that can grow on foods, such as grains and nuts, that have not been stored properly)

statement: Ewing sarcoma is a type of tumor that forms from a certain kind of cell in bone or soft tissue.
source_span: Ewing sarcoma is a type of tumor that forms from a certain kind of cell in bone or soft tissue.

statement: Ewing sarcoma is most common in adolescents and young adults.
source_span: Ewing sarcoma is most common in adolescents and young adults.

statement: Ewing sarcoma has also been called peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor, Askin tumor, extraosseous Ewing sarcoma, and Ewing sarcoma family of tumors.
source_span: Ewing sarcoma has also been called peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor, Askin tumor (Ewing sarcoma of the chest wall), extraosseous Ewing sarcoma (Ewing sarcoma in tissue other than bone), and Ewing sarcoma family of tumors.

statement: Ewing sarcoma may be found in the bones of the legs, arms, feet, hands, chest, pelvis, spine, or skull.
source_span: Ewing sarcoma may be found in the bones of the legs, arms, feet, hands, chest, pelvis, spine, or skull.

statement: For bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, a hollow needle is inserted into the hipbone and samples are removed from both hipbones.
source_span: The removal of bone marrow and a small piece of bone by inserting a hollow needle into the hipbone. Samples are removed from both hipbones.

statement: In a PET scan, radioactive glucose is injected into a vein, and malignant tumor cells show up brighter because they take up more glucose than normal cells.
source_span: A small amount of radioactive glucose (sugar) is injected into a vein...Malignant tumor cells show up brighter in the picture because they are more active and take up more glucose than normal cells do.

statement: Three types of biopsy may be used to diagnose Ewing sarcoma: needle biopsy, incisional biopsy, and excisional biopsy.
source_span: Needle biopsy...Incisional biopsy...Excisional biopsy

statement: A complete blood count (CBC) checks the number of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, and the amount of hemoglobin in red blood cells.
source_span: Complete blood count (CBC): A procedure in which a sample of blood is drawn and checked for the following: - The number of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - The amount of hemoglobin (the protein that carries oxygen) in the red blood cells.

statement: Osteosarcoma usually starts in osteoblasts, a type of bone cell that becomes new bone tissue.
source_span: Osteosarcoma usually starts in osteoblasts, which are a type of bone cell that becomes new bone tissue.

statement: Osteosarcoma is most common in adolescents and often forms in the bones near the knee in children and adolescents.
source_span: Osteosarcoma is most common in adolescents...In children and adolescents, it often forms in the bones near the knee.

statement: Osteosarcoma is the most common type of bone cancer.
source_span: Osteosarcoma is the most common type of bone cancer.

statement: Malignant fibrous histiocytoma (MFH) of bone is a rare tumor of the bone that is treated like osteosarcoma.
source_span: Malignant fibrous histiocytoma (MFH) of bone is a rare tumor of the bone. It is treated like osteosarcoma.

statement: Risk factors for osteosarcoma include past radiation therapy, past treatment with alkylating agents, a change in the retinoblastoma gene, and conditions such as Bloom syndrome, Diamond-Blackfan anemia, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Paget disease, hereditary retinoblastoma, Rothmund-Thomson syndrome, and Werner syndrome.
source_span: Risk factors for osteosarcoma include the following: - Past treatment with radiation therapy. - Past treatment with anticancer drugs called alkylating agents. - Having a certain change in the retinoblastoma gene. - Having certain conditions, such as the following: Bloom syndrome. Diamond-Blackfan anemia. Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Paget disease. Hereditary retinoblastoma. Rothmund-Thomson syndrome. Werner syndrome.

statement: Signs and symptoms of osteosarcoma and MFH include swelling over a bone, joint pain, and a bone that breaks for no known reason.
source_span: Check with a doctor if your child has any of the following: - Swelling over a bone or bony part of the body. - Pain in a bone or joint. - A bone that breaks for no known reason.

statement: Two types of biopsy may be used to diagnose osteosarcoma: core biopsy and incisional biopsy.
source_span: There are two types of biopsy that may be used: - Core biopsy: The removal of tissue using a wide needle. - Incisional biopsy: The removal of part of a lump or a sample of tissue that doesn't look normal.

statement: After treatment, prognosis depends partly on whether chemotherapy is delayed more than 3 weeks after surgery and whether the cancer recurred within 2 years of diagnosis.
source_span: Whether chemotherapy is delayed for more than 3 weeks after surgery takes place. - Whether the cancer has recurred (come back) within 2 years of diagnosis.

statement: A gastrointestinal carcinoid tumor is cancer that forms in the lining of the gastrointestinal tract.
source_span: A gastrointestinal carcinoid tumor is cancer that forms in the lining of the gastrointestinal tract.

statement: The GI tract is made up of the stomach, small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), colon, and rectum.
source_span: Stomach.    -  Small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, and ileum).    -  Colon.    -  Rectum.

statement: GI carcinoid tumors form from neuroendocrine cells scattered throughout the chest and abdomen, most found in the GI tract.
source_span: Gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors form from a certain type of neuroendocrine cell (a type of cell that is like a nerve cell and a hormone-making cell). These cells are scattered throughout the chest and abdomen but most are found in the GI tract.

statement: GI carcinoid tumors are rare and most grow very slowly, occurring mostly in the small intestine, rectum, and appendix.
source_span: GI carcinoid tumors are rare and most grow very slowly. Most of them occur in the small intestine, rectum, and appendix.

statement: Carcinoid syndrome may occur if the tumor spreads to the liver or other parts of the body, or if tumor cells enter the blood.
source_span: Carcinoid syndrome may occur if the tumor spreads to the liver or other parts of the body...This can also happen if tumor cells enter the blood.

statement: Signs and symptoms of carcinoid syndrome include redness/warmth in the face and neck, abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, wheezing or trouble breathing, and fast heartbeat.
source_span: Redness or a feeling of warmth in the face and neck. - Abdominal pain. - Feeling bloated. - Diarrhea. - Wheezing or other trouble breathing. - Fast heartbeat.

statement: Risk factors for GI carcinoid tumors include having a family history of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) syndrome or neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) syndrome.
source_span: Having a family history of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) syndrome or neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) syndrome.

statement: Risk factors for GI carcinoid tumors also include conditions affecting stomach acid production, such as atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, or Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
source_span: Having certain conditions that affect the stomach's ability to make stomach acid, such as atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, or Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

statement: Some GI carcinoid tumors, especially of the stomach or appendix, cause no signs or symptoms and are often found during tests or treatments for other conditions.
source_span: Some tumors, especially tumors of the stomach or appendix, may not cause signs or symptoms. Carcinoid tumors are often found during tests or treatments for other conditions.

statement: Signs and symptoms of GI carcinoid tumors in the rectum include blood in the stool, pain in the rectum, and constipation.
source_span: Signs and symptoms of GI carcinoid tumors in the rectum may include the following: -  Blood in the stool.       - Pain in the rectum.       -  Constipation.

statement: Myeloproliferative neoplasms are a group of diseases in which the bone marrow makes too many red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets.
source_span: Myeloproliferative neoplasms are a group of diseases in which the bone marrow makes too many red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets.

statement: There are 6 types of chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms.
source_span: There are 6 types of chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms.

statement: The 6 types of chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms are chronic myelogenous leukemia, polycythemia vera, primary myelofibrosis (also called chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis), essential thrombocythemia, chronic neutrophilic leukemia, and chronic eosinophilic leukemia.
source_span: Chronic myelogenous leukemia.    -  Polycythemia vera.    -  Primary myelofibrosis (also called chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis).     -  Essential thrombocythemia.    -  Chronic neutrophilic leukemia.    -  Chronic eosinophilic leukemia.

statement: Chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms sometimes become acute leukemia, in which too many abnormal white blood cells are made.
source_span: Chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms sometimes become acute leukemia, in which too many abnormal white blood cells are made.

statement: There is no standard staging system for chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms.
source_span: There is no standard staging system for chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms.

statement: A JAK2 gene mutation is often found in patients with polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, or primary myelofibrosis.
source_span: A JAK2 gene mutation is often found in patients with polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, or primary myelofibrosis.

statement: MPL or CALR gene mutations are found in patients with essential thrombocythemia or primary myelofibrosis.
source_span: MPL or CALR gene mutations are found in patients with essential thrombocythemia or primary myelofibrosis.

statement: There are eleven types of standard treatment for chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms, including watchful waiting, phlebotomy, platelet apheresis, transfusion therapy, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, other drug therapy, surgery, biologic therapy, targeted therapy, and high-dose chemotherapy with stem cell transplant.
source_span: Eleven types of standard treatment are used:          - Watchful waiting     -  Phlebotomy      -  Platelet apheresis      - Transfusion therapy     -  Chemotherapy      -  Radiation therapy      - Other drug therapy     -  Surgery      - Biologic therapy      - Targeted therapy     - High-dose chemotherapy with stem cell transplant

statement: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy involves removing bone marrow, blood, and a small piece of bone by inserting a hollow needle into the hipbone or breastbone.
source_span: The removal of bone marrow, blood, and a small piece of bone by inserting a hollow needle into the hipbone or breastbone.

statement: Polycythemia vera is a disease in which too many red blood cells are made in the bone marrow.
source_span: Polycythemia vera is a disease in which too many red blood cells are made in the bone marrow.

statement: In patients older than 65 years or with a history of blood clots, the risk of stroke or heart attack from polycythemia vera is higher.
source_span: In patients who are older than 65 years or who have a history of blood clots, the risk of stroke or heart attack is higher.

statement: Patients with polycythemia vera have an increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia or primary myelofibrosis.
source_span: Patients also have an increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia or primary myelofibrosis.

statement: Symptoms of polycythemia vera include headaches and a feeling of fullness below the ribs on the left side.
source_span: Symptoms of polycythemia vera include headaches and a feeling of fullness below the ribs on the left side.

statement: Other symptoms of polycythemia vera include double vision or seeing dark/blind spots, itching all over the body especially after warm or hot water, a reddened face, weakness, dizziness, and unexplained weight loss.
source_span: Double vision or seeing dark or blind spots that come and go.    - Itching all over the body, especially after being in warm or hot water.    - Reddened face that looks like a blush or sunburn.    - Weakness.    - Dizziness.    - Weight loss for no known reason.

statement: A serum erythropoietin test is used to diagnose polycythemia vera.
source_span: a serum erythropoietin test is used to diagnose polycythemia vera

statement: In polycythemia vera, the erythropoietin level is lower than normal because the body does not need to make more red blood cells.
source_span: In polycythemia vera, the erythropoietin level would be lower than normal because the body does not need to make more red blood cells.

statement: Treatment of polycythemia vera may include phlebotomy, chemotherapy with or without phlebotomy, biologic therapy using interferon alfa or pegylated interferon alpha, and low-dose aspirin.
source_span: Phlebotomy.     -  Chemotherapy with or without phlebotomy.     -  Biologic therapy using interferon alfa or pegylated interferon alpha.     - Low-dose aspirin.

statement: Primary myelofibrosis is a disease in which abnormal blood cells and fibers build up inside the bone marrow.
source_span: Primary myelofibrosis is a disease in which abnormal blood cells and fibers build up inside the bone marrow.

statement: Primary myelofibrosis is also called chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis.
source_span: In primary myelofibrosis (also called chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis)

statement: In primary myelofibrosis, the web of fibers inside the bone marrow becomes very thick like scar tissue and slows the blood-forming tissue's ability to make blood cells.
source_span: The web of fibers inside the bone marrow also becomes very thick (like scar tissue) and slows the blood-forming tissues ability to make blood cells.

statement: To make up for the low number of blood cells made in the bone marrow, the liver and spleen begin to make blood cells.
source_span: In order to make up for the low number of blood cells made in the bone marrow, the liver and spleen begin to make the blood cells.

statement: Symptoms of primary myelofibrosis include pain below the ribs on the left side and feeling very tired.
source_span: Symptoms of primary myelofibrosis include pain below the ribs on the left side and feeling very tired.

statement: Primary myelofibrosis often does not cause early signs or symptoms and may be found during a routine blood test.
source_span: Primary myelofibrosis often does not cause early signs or symptoms. It may be found during a routine blood test.

statement: Prognosis for primary myelofibrosis depends on the age of the patient, the number of abnormal red and white blood cells, the number of blasts in the blood, whether there are certain chromosome changes, and whether the patient has fever, night sweats, or weight loss.
source_span: The age of the patient.    - The number of abnormal red blood cells and white blood cells.    - The number of blasts in the blood.    - Whether there are certain changes in the chromosomes.    - Whether the patient has signs such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss.

statement: Treatment of primary myelofibrosis in patients without signs or symptoms is usually watchful waiting.
source_span: Treatment of primary myelofibrosis in patients without signs or symptoms is usually watchful waiting.

statement: Anemia in primary myelofibrosis is usually treated with transfusion of red blood cells, and may also be treated with erythropoietic growth factors, prednisone, danazol, or thalidomide/lenalidomide/pomalidomide with or without prednisone.
source_span: Anemia is usually treated with transfusion of red blood cells to relieve symptoms and improve quality of life. In addition, anemia may be treated with: -  Erythropoietic growth factors.     -  Prednisone.     -  Danazol.     -  Thalidomide, lenalidomide, or pomalidomide, with or without prednisone.

statement: Treatment of primary myelofibrosis in patients with other signs or symptoms may include targeted therapy with ruxolitinib, chemotherapy, donor stem cell transplant, splenectomy, radiation therapy, or biologic therapy with interferon alfa.
source_span: Targeted therapy with ruxolitinib.     -  Chemotherapy.     -  Donor stem cell transplant. ... -  Splenectomy.     -  Radiation therapy to the spleen, lymph nodes, or other areas ... -  Biologic therapy using interferon alfa or erythropoietic growth factors.

statement: Essential thrombocythemia is a disease in which too many platelets are made in the bone marrow.
source_span: Essential thrombocythemia is a disease in which too many platelets are made in the bone marrow.

statement: Essential thrombocythemia causes an abnormal increase in the number of platelets made in the blood and bone marrow.
source_span: Essential thrombocythemia causes an abnormal increase in the number of platelets made in the blood and bone marrow.

statement: Patients with essential thrombocythemia may have no signs or symptoms, and it is often found during a routine blood test.
source_span: Patients with essential thrombocythemia may have no signs or symptoms. Essential thrombocythemia often does not cause early signs or symptoms. It may be found during a routine blood test.

statement: Symptoms of essential thrombocythemia include headache, burning or tingling in the hands or feet, redness and warmth of the hands or feet, and vision or hearing problems.
source_span: Headache.    - Burning or tingling in the hands or feet.    - Redness and warmth of the hands or feet.    - Vision or hearing problems.

statement: When there are too many platelets, they may clump together and make it hard for blood to flow, and clots may form in blood vessels, causing serious health problems such as stroke or heart attack.
source_span: When there are too many platelets, they may clump together and make it hard for the blood to flow. Clots may form in blood vessels and there may also be increased bleeding. These can cause serious health problems such as stroke or heart attack.

statement: Prognosis and treatment options for essential thrombocythemia depend on the age of the patient and whether the patient has signs or symptoms or other related problems.
source_span: The age of the patient.    - Whether the patient has signs or symptoms or other problems related to essential thrombocythemia.

statement: Treatment of essential thrombocythemia in patients younger than 60 years with no signs or symptoms and an acceptable platelet count is usually watchful waiting.
source_span: Treatment of essential thrombocythemia in patients younger than 60 years who have no signs or symptoms and an acceptable platelet count is usually watchful waiting.

statement: Treatment options for other essential thrombocythemia patients may include chemotherapy, anagrelide therapy, biologic therapy with interferon alfa or pegylated interferon alpha, and platelet apheresis.
source_span: Chemotherapy.     -  Anagrelide therapy.     -  Biologic therapy using interferon alfa or pegylated interferon alpha.     - Platelet apheresis.

statement: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia is a disease in which too many white blood cells (eosinophils) are made in the bone marrow.
source_span: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia is a disease in which too many white blood cells (eosinophils) are made in the bone marrow.

statement: Eosinophils are white blood cells that react to allergens and help fight infections caused by certain parasites.
source_span: Eosinophils are white blood cells that react to allergens (substances that cause an allergic response) and help fight infections caused by certain parasites.

statement: In chronic eosinophilic leukemia, there are too many eosinophils in the blood, bone marrow, and other tissues.
source_span: In chronic eosinophilic leukemia, there are too many eosinophils in the blood, bone marrow, and other tissues.

statement: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia may stay the same for many years or may progress quickly to acute leukemia.
source_span: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia may stay the same for many years or it may progress quickly to acute leukemia.

statement: Signs and symptoms of chronic eosinophilic leukemia include fever and feeling very tired.
source_span: Signs and symptoms of chronic eosinophilic leukemia include fever and feeling very tired.

statement: Other symptoms of chronic eosinophilic leukemia include cough, swelling under the skin around the eyes, lips, throat, hands, or feet, muscle pain, itching, and diarrhea.
source_span: Cough.    - Swelling under the skin around the eyes and lips, in the throat, or on the hands and feet.    - Muscle pain.    - Itching.    -  Diarrhea.

statement: Treatment of chronic eosinophilic leukemia may include bone marrow transplant, biologic therapy using interferon alfa, or a clinical trial of a new treatment.
source_span: Bone marrow transplant.     -  Biologic therapy using interferon alfa.     - A clinical trial of a new treatment.

Myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms are diseases in which the bone marrow makes too many white blood cells.
source_span: the bone marrow makes too many white blood cells

statement: Myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms have features of both myelodysplastic syndromes and myeloproliferative neoplasms.
source_span: have features of both myelodysplastic syndromes and myeloproliferative neoplasms

statement: The 3 main types of myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms are chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML), juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML), and atypical chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML).
source_span: Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML).    -  Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML).    - Atypical chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML)

statement: When a myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm does not match any of the 3 main types, it is called MDS/MPN, unclassifiable (MDS/MPN-UC).
source_span: it is called myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm, unclassifiable (MDS/MPN-UC)

statement: Myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms may progress to acute leukemia.
source_span: Myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms may progress to acute leukemia.

statement: There is no standard staging system for myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms.
source_span: There is no standard staging system for myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms.

statement: Five types of standard treatment for myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms are chemotherapy, other drug therapy, stem cell transplant, supportive care, and targeted therapy.
source_span: Chemotherapy      - Other drug therapy     - Stem cell transplant     -  Supportive care      - Targeted therapy

statement: The cancer cells in myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms do not contain the Philadelphia chromosome that is present in chronic myelogenous leukemia.
source_span: do not contain the Philadelphia chromosome that is present in chronic myelogenous leukemia

statement: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy involves removing a small piece of bone and bone marrow by inserting a needle into the hipbone or breastbone.
source_span: The removal of a small piece of bone and bone marrow by inserting a needle into the hipbone or breastbone.

statement: Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) is a disease in which too many myelocytes and monocytes (immature white blood cells) are made in the bone marrow.
source_span: too many myelocytes and monocytes (immature white blood cells) are made in the bone marrow

statement: Older age and being male increase the risk of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia.
source_span: Older age and being male increase the risk of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia.

statement: Possible risk factors for CMML include older age, being male, being exposed to certain substances at work or in the environment, being exposed to radiation, and past treatment with certain anticancer drugs.
source_span: Being exposed to certain substances at work or in the environment.    - Being exposed to radiation.    - Past treatment with certain anticancer drugs.

statement: Signs and symptoms of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia include fever, weight loss, and feeling very tired.
source_span: Signs and symptoms of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia include fever, weight loss, and feeling very tired.

statement: Prognosis and treatment options for CMML depend on white blood cell or platelet counts, whether the patient is anemic, the amount of blasts, the amount of hemoglobin, and whether there are certain chromosome changes.
source_span: The prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options for CMML depend on the following:         - The number of white blood cells or platelets in the blood or bone marrow.    - Whether the patient is anemic.    - The amount of blasts in the blood or bone marrow.    - The amount of hemoglobin in red blood cells.    - Whether there are certain changes in the chromosomes.

statement: Treatment of CMML may include chemotherapy with one or more agents, stem cell transplant, or a clinical trial of a new treatment.
source_span: Treatment of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) may include the following:         -  Chemotherapy with one or more agents.    -  Stem cell transplant.    - A clinical trial of a new treatment.

statement: Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) is a childhood disease in which too many myelocytes and monocytes (immature white blood cells) are made in the bone marrow.
source_span: Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia is a childhood disease in which too many myelocytes and monocytes (immature white blood cells) are made in the bone marrow.

statement: JMML is a rare childhood cancer that occurs more often in children younger than 2 years.
source_span: occurs more often in children younger than 2 years

statement: Children who have neurofibromatosis type 1 and males have an increased risk of juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia.
source_span: Children who have neurofibromatosis type 1 and males have an increased risk of juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia.

statement: Signs and symptoms of JMML include fever, weight loss, and feeling very tired.
source_span: Signs and symptoms of juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia include fever, weight loss, and feeling very tired.

statement: Other JMML symptoms can include infections such as bronchitis or tonsillitis, easy bruising or bleeding, skin rash, and painless swelling of lymph nodes in the neck, underarm, stomach, or groin.
source_span: Painless swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck, underarm, stomach, or groin.

statement: Prognosis and treatment options for JMML depend on the age of the child at diagnosis, the number of platelets in the blood, and the amount of a certain type of hemoglobin in red blood cells.
source_span: The prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options for JMML depend on the following:         - The age of the child at diagnosis.    - The number of platelets in the blood.    - The amount of a certain type of hemoglobin in red blood cells.

statement: Treatment of JMML may include combination chemotherapy, stem cell transplant, 13-cis-retinoic acid therapy, or a clinical trial such as targeted therapy.
source_span: Combination chemotherapy.    -  Stem cell transplant.    -  13-cis-retinoic acid therapy.    - A clinical trial of a new treatment, such as targeted therapy.

statement: Atypical chronic myelogenous leukemia is a disease in which too many granulocytes (immature white blood cells) are made in the bone marrow.
source_span: Atypical chronic myelogenous leukemia is a disease in which too many granulocytes (immature white blood cells) are made in the bone marrow.

statement: In atypical CML, the body tells too many blood stem cells to become granulocytes; some never mature and are called blasts.
source_span: the body tells too many blood stem cells to become a type of white blood cell called granulocytes. Some of these blood stem cells never become mature white blood cells. These immature white blood cells are called blasts.

statement: Over time, granulocytes and blasts crowd out red blood cells and platelets in the bone marrow.
source_span: Over time, the granulocytes and blasts crowd out the red blood cells and platelets in the bone marrow.

statement: Leukemia cells in atypical CML look like those in CML under a microscope, but atypical CML lacks the Philadelphia chromosome change.
source_span: in atypical CML a certain chromosome change, called the "Philadelphia chromosome" is not there.

statement: Signs and symptoms of atypical CML include easy bruising or bleeding and feeling tired and weak.
source_span: Signs and symptoms of atypical chronic myelogenous leukemia include easy bruising or bleeding and feeling tired and weak.

statement: Symptoms to check with a doctor about include shortness of breath, pale skin, petechiae, and pain or fullness below the ribs on the left side.
source_span: Shortness of breath. - Pale skin. - Feeling very tired and weak. - Easy bruising or bleeding. - Petechiae (flat, pinpoint spots under the skin caused by bleeding). - Pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs on the left side.

statement: The prognosis for atypical CML depends on the number of red blood cells and platelets in the blood.
source_span: The prognosis (chance of recovery) for atypical CML depends on the number of red blood cells and platelets in the blood.

statement: Treatment of atypical CML may include chemotherapy.
source_span: Treatment of atypical chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) may include chemotherapy.

statement: MDS/MPN-UC has features of both myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative diseases but is not chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, or atypical chronic myelogenous leukemia.
source_span: is a disease that has features of both myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative diseases but is not chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, or atypical chronic myelogenous leukemia.

statement: Signs and symptoms of MDS/MPN-UC include fever, weight loss, and feeling very tired.
source_span: Signs and symptoms of myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm, unclassifiable, include fever, weight loss, and feeling very tired.

statement: In MDS/MPN-UC, blood stem cells are told to become red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets, and some never mature, becoming blasts that crowd out healthy blood cells.
source_span: the body tells too many blood stem cells to become red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets. Some of these blood stem cells never become mature blood cells. These immature blood cells are called blasts.

statement: MDS/MPN-UC is a very rare disease, so the factors that affect risk and prognosis are not known.
source_span: MDS/MPN-UC is a very rare disease. Because it is so rare, the factors that affect risk and prognosis are not known.

statement: Symptoms to check with a doctor about include fever or frequent infections, shortness of breath, pale skin, easy bruising or bleeding, petechiae, and pain or fullness below the ribs.
source_span: Fever or frequent infections. - Shortness of breath. - Feeling very tired and weak. - Pale skin. - Easy bruising or bleeding. - Petechiae (flat, pinpoint spots under the skin caused by bleeding). - Pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs.

statement: Treatment of MDS/MPN-UC may include supportive care and targeted therapy with imatinib mesylate.
source_span: Supportive care treatments to manage problems caused by the disease such as infection, bleeding, and anemia. - Targeted therapy (imatinib mesylate).

statement: Endometrial cancer is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the endometrium.
source_span: Endometrial cancer is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the endometrium.

statement: Obesity and having metabolic syndrome may increase the risk of endometrial cancer.
source_span: Obesity and having metabolic syndrome may increase the risk of endometrial cancer.

statement: Metabolic syndrome includes extra fat around the abdomen, high blood sugar, high blood pressure, high triglycerides, and low HDL levels in the blood.
source_span: Having metabolic syndrome, a set of conditions that occur together, including extra fat around the abdomen, high blood sugar, high blood pressure, high levels of triglycerides and low levels of high-density lipoproteins in the blood.

statement: Endometrial cancer may develop in breast cancer patients who have been treated with tamoxifen.
source_span: Endometrial cancer may develop in breast cancer patients who have been treated with tamoxifen.

statement: Women taking estrogen alone (without progesterone) have an increased risk of endometrial cancer, but taking estrogen combined with progesterone does not increase that risk.
source_span: Women taking estrogen (a hormone that can affect the growth of some cancers) alone also have an increased risk of endometrial cancer. Taking estrogen combined with progesterone (another hormone) does not increase a womans risk of endometrial cancer.

statement: Other risk factors for endometrial cancer include endometrial hyperplasia, never giving birth, early menstruation, late menopause, PCOS, family history of uterine cancer, a Lynch syndrome-linked gene change, and hyperinsulinemia.
source_span: Having endometrial hyperplasia. - Being obese. ... Never giving birth. - Beginning menstruation at an early age. - Reaching menopause at an older age. - Having polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). - Having a mother, sister, or daughter with uterine cancer. - Having a certain gene change that is linked to Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer). - Having hyperinsulinemia (high levels of insulin in the blood).

statement: Symptoms of endometrial cancer include vaginal bleeding or discharge unrelated to menstruation, vaginal bleeding after menopause, difficult or painful urination, pain during sexual intercourse, and pain in the pelvic area.
source_span: Vaginal bleeding or discharge not related to menstruation (periods). - Vaginal bleeding after menopause. - Difficult or painful urination. - Pain during sexual intercourse. - Pain in the pelvic area.

statement: Endometrial cancer does not usually show up in Pap test results, so a sample of endometrial tissue must be removed and examined under a microscope.
source_span: Because endometrial cancer begins inside the uterus, it does not usually show up in the results of a Pap test. For this reason, a sample of endometrial tissue must be removed and checked under a microscope to look for cancer cells.

statement: Dilatation and curettage (D&C) is a procedure in which the cervix is dilated and a spoon-shaped instrument called a curette is inserted into the uterus to remove tissue samples from the inner lining.
source_span: A procedure to remove samples of tissue from the inner lining of the uterus. The cervix is dilated and a curette (spoon-shaped instrument) is inserted into the uterus to remove tissue.

statement: Extragonadal germ cell tumors form from developing sperm or egg cells that travel from the gonads to other parts of the body.
source_span: Extragonadal germ cell tumors form from developing sperm or egg cells that travel from the gonads to other parts of the body.

statement: "Extragonadal" means outside of the gonads (sex organs).
source_span: " Extragonadal" means outside of the gonads (sex organs).

statement: Extragonadal germ cell tumors usually begin in organs such as the pineal gland in the brain, the mediastinum, or the retroperitoneum.
source_span: usually begin in organs such as the pineal gland in the brain, in the mediastinum (area between the lungs), or in the retroperitoneum (the back wall of the abdomen)

statement: Benign extragonadal germ cell tumors are called benign teratomas and are more common than malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors.
source_span: Benign extragonadal germ cell tumors are called benign teratomas. These are more common than malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors

statement: Malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors are divided into two types: nonseminoma and seminoma.
source_span: Malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors are divided into two types, nonseminoma and seminoma.

statement: Nonseminomas tend to grow and spread more quickly than seminomas.
source_span: Nonseminomas tend to grow and spread more quickly than seminomas.

statement: If untreated, malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors may spread to the lungs, lymph nodes, bones, liver, or other parts of the body.
source_span: If untreated, malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors may spread to the lungs, lymph nodes, bones, liver, or other parts of the body.

statement: Risk factors for malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors include being male, being age 20 or older, and having Klinefelter syndrome.
source_span: Risk factors for malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors include the following: - Being male. - Being age 20 or older. - Having Klinefelter syndrome.

statement: Signs and symptoms of extragonadal germ cell tumors include chest pain, breathing problems, cough, fever, headache, change in bowel habits, feeling very tired, trouble walking, and trouble seeing or moving the eyes.
source_span: Chest pain. - Breathing problems. - Cough. - Fever. - Headache. - Change in bowel habits. - Feeling very tired. - Trouble walking. - Trouble in seeing or moving the eyes.

statement: Three tumor markers used to detect extragonadal germ cell tumors are Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG), and Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH).
source_span: The following three tumor markers are used to detect extragonadal germ cell tumor: - Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). - Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (-hCG). - Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH).

statement: Prognosis and treatment options for extragonadal germ cell tumors depend on tumor type (nonseminoma/seminoma), size and location, AFP/hCG/LDH blood levels, whether it has spread, treatment response, and whether newly diagnosed or recurred.
source_span: The prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options depend on the following: - Whether the tumor is nonseminoma or seminoma. - The size of the tumor and where it is in the body. - The blood levels of AFP, -hCG, and LDH. - Whether the tumor has spread to other parts of the body. - The way the tumor responds to initial treatment. - Whether the tumor has just been diagnosed or has recurred (come back).

statement: Intraocular melanoma is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the eye.
source_span: Intraocular melanoma is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the eye.

statement: Intraocular melanoma forms in the middle layer of the eye wall, called the uvea or uveal tract, which has three main parts: the iris, ciliary body, and choroid.
source_span: The middle layer, where intraocular melanoma forms, is called the uvea or uveal tract, and has three main parts: - Iris ... - Ciliary body ... - Choroid

statement: Most intraocular melanomas begin in the choroid.
source_span: Most intraocular melanomas begin in the choroid.

statement: Intraocular melanoma is the most common eye cancer in adults.
source_span: It is the most common eye cancer in adults.

statement: Intraocular melanoma of the iris is usually a small tumor that grows slowly and rarely spreads to other parts of the body.
source_span: Intraocular melanoma of the iris is usually a small tumor that grows slowly and rarely spreads to other parts of the body.

statement: Risk factors for intraocular melanoma include fair complexion (fair skin that freckles/burns easily, blue/green/light-colored eyes), older age, and being white.
source_span: Risk factors for intraocular melanoma include the following: - Having a fair complexion...- Older age. - Being white.

statement: Signs of intraocular melanoma include blurred vision, floaters or flashes of light, a dark spot on the iris, a change in pupil size/shape, and a change in eyeball position.
source_span: Blurred vision or other change in vision. - Floaters ... or flashes of light. - A dark spot on the iris. - A change in the size or shape of the pupil. - A change in the position of the eyeball in the eye socket.

statement: A biopsy of the tumor is rarely needed to diagnose intraocular melanoma.
source_span: A biopsy of the tumor is rarely needed to diagnose intraocular melanoma.

statement: Retinoblastoma is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the retina.
source_span: Retinoblastoma is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the retina.

statement: Retinoblastoma occurs most often in children younger than 2 years.
source_span: it occurs most often in children younger than 2 years

statement: Retinoblastoma may be unilateral (one eye) or bilateral (both eyes) and rarely spreads from the eye to nearby tissue or other parts of the body.
source_span: The cancer may be in one eye (unilateral) or in both eyes (bilateral). Retinoblastoma rarely spreads from the eye to nearby tissue or other parts of the body.

statement: A child is thought to have heritable retinoblastoma if there is a family history, a mutation in the RB1 gene, more than one tumor or tumors in both eyes, or a tumor in one eye with the child younger than 1 year.
source_span: A child is thought to have the heritable form of retinoblastoma when one of the following is true: - There is a family history of retinoblastoma. - There is a certain mutation (change) in the RB1 gene. ... - There is more than one tumor in the eye or there is a tumor in both eyes. - There is a tumor in one eye and the child is younger than 1 year.

statement: Most cases of retinoblastoma are the nonheritable form.
source_span: Most cases of retinoblastoma are the nonheritable form.

statement: After heritable retinoblastoma is diagnosed and treated, regular eye exams to check for new tumors are usually done every 2 to 4 months for at least 28 months.
source_span: Regular eye exams to check for new tumors are usually done every 2 to 4 months for at least 28 months.

statement: Brothers or sisters of a child with retinoblastoma should have regular eye exams by an ophthalmologist until age 3 to 5 years, unless known they lack the RB1 gene change.
source_span: Brothers or sisters of a child with retinoblastoma should have regular eye exams by an ophthalmologist until age 3 to 5 years, unless it is known that the brother or sister does not have the RB1 gene change.

statement: Trilateral retinoblastoma is when retinoblastoma and a pineal brain tumor occur at the same time; the brain tumor is usually diagnosed between 20 and 36 months of age.
source_span: When retinoblastoma and a brain tumor occur at the same time, it is called trilateral retinoblastoma. The brain tumor is usually diagnosed between 20 and 36 months of age.

statement: CT scans are usually not used for routine retinoblastoma screening in order to avoid exposing the child to ionizing radiation.
source_span: CT (computerized tomography) scans are usually not used for routine screening in order to avoid exposing the child to ionizing radiation.

statement: Heritable retinoblastoma increases the child's risk of other cancers in later years, such as lung cancer, bladder cancer, or melanoma.
source_span: Heritable retinoblastoma also increases the child's risk of other types of cancer such as lung cancer, bladder cancer, or melanoma in later years.

statement: A common symptom of retinoblastoma is that the pupil of the eye appears white instead of red when light shines into it, which may be seen in flash photographs.
source_span: Pupil of the eye appears white instead of red when light shines into it. This may be seen in flash photographs of the child.

statement: Uterine sarcoma is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the muscles of the uterus or other tissues that support the uterus.
source_span: Uterine sarcoma is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the muscles of the uterus or other tissues that support the uterus.

statement: Being exposed to x-rays can increase the risk of uterine sarcoma.
source_span: Being exposed to x-rays can increase the risk of uterine sarcoma.

statement: Past treatment with radiation therapy to the pelvis is a risk factor for uterine sarcoma.
source_span: Past treatment with radiation therapy to the pelvis.

statement: Treatment with tamoxifen for breast cancer is a risk factor for uterine sarcoma.
source_span: Treatment with tamoxifen for breast cancer.

statement: Women taking tamoxifen should have a pelvic exam every year and report any vaginal bleeding other than menstrual bleeding as soon as possible.
source_span: have a pelvic exam every year and report any vaginal bleeding (other than menstrual bleeding) as soon as possible.

statement: Signs of uterine sarcoma include bleeding not part of menstrual periods, bleeding after menopause, a mass in the vagina, pain or fullness in the abdomen, and frequent urination.
source_span: Bleeding that is not part of menstrual periods.    - Bleeding after menopause.    - A mass in the vagina.    - Pain or a feeling of fullness in the abdomen.    - Frequent urination.

statement: The CA 125 assay is a test used in staging that measures the level of CA 125 in the blood.
source_span: CA 125 assay : A test that measures the level of CA 125 in the blood.

statement: Uterine sarcoma may be diagnosed, staged, and treated in the same surgery.
source_span: Uterine sarcoma may be diagnosed, staged, and treated in the same surgery.

statement: There are four stages of uterine sarcoma: Stage I, Stage II, Stage III, and Stage IV.
source_span: The following stages are used for uterine sarcoma:         - Stage I     - Stage II     - Stage III     - Stage IV

statement: Prognosis and treatment options for uterine sarcoma depend on the stage of the cancer, the type and size of the tumor, the patient's general health, and whether the cancer is newly diagnosed or recurred.
source_span: The stage of the cancer.    - The type and size of the tumor.    - The patient's general health.    - Whether the cancer has just been diagnosed or has recurred (come back).

statement: Dilatation and curettage (D&C) is a procedure to remove samples of tissue from the inner lining of the uterus, using a curette after the cervix is dilated.
source_span: Dilatation and curettage : A procedure to remove samples of tissue from the inner lining of the uterus. The cervix is dilated and a curette (spoon-shaped instrument) is inserted into the uterus to remove tissue.

statement: Because uterine sarcoma begins inside the uterus, it may not show up on a Pap test.
source_span: Because uterine sarcoma begins inside the uterus, this cancer may not show up on the Pap test.

statement: Endometrial cancer is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the endometrium.
source_span: Endometrial cancer is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the endometrium.

statement: Endometrial cancer is the most common invasive cancer of the female reproductive system.
source_span: Endometrial cancer is the most common invasive cancer of the female reproductive system.

statement: Endometrial cancer is diagnosed most often in postmenopausal women at an average age of 60 years.
source_span: Endometrial cancer is diagnosed most often in postmenopausal women at an average age of 60 years

statement: From 2004 to 2013, the number of new cases of endometrial cancer increased slightly in white and African American women.
source_span: From 2004 to 2013, the number of new cases of endometrial cancer increased slightly in white and African American women.

statement: From 2005 to 2014, the number of deaths from endometrial cancer also increased slightly in white and African American women.
source_span: From 2005 to 2014, the number of deaths from endometrial cancer also increased slightly in white and African American women.

statement: Compared with white women, rates of endometrial cancer are lower in Japanese Americans and Latinas.
source_span: Compared with white women, rates of endometrial cancer are lower in Japanese Americans and in Latinas.

statement: The number of deaths from endometrial cancer is higher in African American women compared with women of other races.
source_span: The number of deaths from endometrial cancer is higher in African American women compared with women of other races.

statement: Using tamoxifen for more than 2 years increases the risk of endometrial cancer, and this risk is greater in postmenopausal women.
source_span: using tamoxifen for more than 2 years increases the risk of endometrial cancer. This risk is greater in postmenopausal women.

statement: Raloxifene does not have estrogen-like effects on the uterus and has not been shown to increase the risk of endometrial cancer.
source_span: it does not have estrogen-like effects on the uterus and has not been shown to increase the risk of endometrial cancer.

statement: For postmenopausal women, taking estrogen in combination with progestin does not increase the risk of endometrial cancer, but does increase the risk of breast cancer.
source_span: taking estrogen in combination with progestin does not increase the risk of endometrial cancer, but it does increase the risk of breast cancer.

statement: Estrogen-only hormone replacement therapy (HRT) increases the risk of endometrial cancer and endometrial hyperplasia, and also increases the risk of stroke and blood clots.
source_span: The use of HRT that contains only estrogen increases the risk of endometrial cancer and endometrial hyperplasia... HRT that contains only estrogen also increases the risk of stroke and blood clots.

statement: Protective factors that decrease the risk of endometrial cancer include pregnancy and breast-feeding, combination oral contraceptives, physical activity, and cigarette smoking.
source_span: The following protective factors decrease the risk of endometrial cancer:         - Pregnancy and breast-feeding     - Combination oral contraceptives     - Physical activity     - Cigarette smoking

statement: Hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC) syndrome, also known as Lynch Syndrome, is an inherited disorder that gives women who have it a much higher risk of developing endometrial cancer.
source_span: Hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC) syndrome (also known as Lynch Syndrome) is an inherited disorder caused by changes in certain genes. Women who have HNPCC syndrome have a much higher risk of developing endometri

statement: Childhood extracranial germ cell tumors form from germ cells in parts of the body other than the brain.
source_span: Childhood extracranial germ cell tumors form from germ cells in parts of the body other than the brain.

statement: Extracranial germ cell tumors usually form in the testicles, ovaries, sacrum or coccyx, retroperitoneum, or mediastinum.
source_span: Extracranial germ cell tumors usually form in the following areas of the body:          - Testicles.    - Ovaries.    -  Sacrum or coccyx (bottom part of the spine).    - Retroperitoneum (the back wall of the abdomen).    -  Mediastinum (area between the lungs).

statement: Extracranial germ cell tumors are most common in adolescents 15 to 19 years of age.
source_span: Extracranial germ cell tumors are most common in adolescents 15 to 19 years of age.

statement: There are three types of extracranial germ cell tumors: mature teratomas, immature teratomas, and malignant germ cell tumors.
source_span: Extracranial germ cell tumors are grouped into mature teratomas, immature teratomas, and malignant germ cell tumors

statement: Mature teratomas are the most common type of extracranial germ cell tumor and are benign, not likely to become cancer.
source_span: Mature teratomas are the most common type of extracranial germ cell tumor. Mature teratomas are benign tumors and not likely to become cancer.

statement: Germinomas are tumors that make a hormone called beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG).
source_span: Germinomas: Tumors that make a hormone called beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (-hCG).

statement: Of the three types of germinomas, dysgerminomas form in the ovary in girls, seminomas form in the testicle in boys, and germinomas form in areas of the body that are not the ovary or testicle.
source_span: Dysgerminomas form in the ovary in girls.       -  Seminomas form in the testicle in boys.       - Germinomas form in areas of the body that are not the ovary or testicle.

statement: Yolk sac tumors make a hormone called alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and can form in the ovary, testicle, or other areas of the body.
source_span: Yolk sac tumors make a hormone called alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). They can form in the ovary, testicle, or other areas of the body.

statement: Choriocarcinomas make a hormone called beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) and can form in the ovary, testicle, or other areas of the body.
source_span: Choriocarcinomas make a hormone called beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (-hCG). They can form in the ovary, testicle, or other areas of the body.

statement: Testicular germ cell tumors usually occur before the age of 4 years or in adolescents and young adults.
source_span: Testicular germ cell tumors usually occur before the age of 4 years or in adolescents and young adults.

statement: Boys older than 14 years with testicular germ cell tumors are treated in pediatric cancer centers, but the treatment is much like the treatment used in adults.
source_span: Boys older than 14 years with testicular germ cell tumors are treated in pediatric cancer centers, but the treatment is much like the treatment used in adults.

statement: Most ovarian germ cell tumors are benign teratomas.
source_span: Most ovarian germ cell tumors are benign teratomas.

statement: Testicular germ cell tumors are divided into two main types: seminoma and nonseminoma.
source_span: Testicular germ cell tumors are divided into two main types, seminoma and nonseminoma.

statement: Ovarian epithelial cancer, fallopian tube cancer, and primary peritoneal cancer are diseases in which malignant cells form in the tissue covering the ovary or lining the fallopian tube or peritoneum.

statement: Ovarian epithelial cancer, fallopian tube cancer, and primary peritoneal cancer form in the same type of tissue and are treated the same way.

statement: Each ovary is about the size and shape of an almond.

statement: Primary peritoneal cancer is cancer that forms in the peritoneum and has not spread there from another part of the body.
source_span: Primary peritoneal cancer is cancer that forms in the peritoneum and has not spread there from another part of the body.

statement: Women who have one first-degree relative (mother, daughter, or sister) with a history of ovarian cancer have an increased risk of ovarian cancer.
source_span: Women who have one first-degree relative (mother, daughter, or sister) with a history of ovarian cancer have an increased risk of ovarian cancer.

statement: The risk of ovarian cancer is even higher in women who have two or more first-degree relatives with a history of ovarian cancer.
source_span: This risk is even higher in women who have two or more first-degree relatives with a history of ovarian cancer.

statement: Hereditary ovarian cancer makes up about 20% of all cases of ovarian cancer.
source_span: Hereditary ovarian cancer makes up about 20% of all cases of ovarian cancer.

statement: There are three hereditary patterns of ovarian cancer: ovarian cancer alone, ovarian and breast cancers, and ovarian and colon cancers.
source_span: There are three hereditary patterns: ovarian cancer alone, ovarian and breast cancers, and ovarian and colon cancers.

statement: A risk-reducing oophorectomy is the removal of healthy ovaries so that cancer cannot grow in them, and in high-risk women this procedure has been shown to greatly decrease the risk of ovarian cancer.
source_span: risk-reducing oophorectomy (the removal of healthy ovaries so that cancer cannot grow in them). In high-risk women, this procedure has been shown to greatly decrease the risk of ovarian cancer.

statement: Signs and symptoms of ovarian, fallopian tube, or peritoneal cancer may include pain, swelling, or pressure in the abdomen or pelvis, heavy or irregular vaginal bleeding especially after menopause, vaginal discharge, a lump in the pelvic area, and gastrointestinal problems such as gas, bloating, or constipation.
source_span: Pain, swelling, or a feeling of pressure in the abdomen or pelvis. Vaginal bleeding that is heavy or irregular, especially after menopause.

statement: Ovarian germ cell tumor is a disease in which malignant cells form in the germ (egg) cells of the ovary.
source_span: malignant (cancer) cells form in the germ (egg) cells of the ovary

statement: Ovarian germ cell tumors usually occur in teenage girls or young women and most often affect just one ovary.
source_span: Ovarian germ cell tumors usually occur in teenage girls or young women and most often affect just one ovary.

statement: The most common ovarian germ cell tumor is called dysgerminoma.
source_span: The most common ovarian germ cell tumor is called dysgerminoma.

statement: Signs of ovarian germ cell tumor are swelling of the abdomen or vaginal bleeding after menopause.
source_span: Signs of ovarian germ cell tumor are swelling of the abdomen or vaginal bleeding after menopause.

statement: An increased level of alpha fetoprotein (AFP) or human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) in the blood may be a sign of ovarian germ cell tumor.
source_span: An increased level of alpha fetoprotein (AFP) or human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) in the blood may be a sign of ovarian germ cell tumor.

statement: Prognosis and treatment options for ovarian germ cell tumor depend on the type of cancer, the size of the tumor, the stage of cancer, how the cancer cells look under a microscope, and the patient's general health.
source_span: The prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options depend on the following: - The type of cancer. - The size of the tumor. - The stage of cancer... - The way the cancer cells look under a microscope. - The patients general health.

statement: Ovarian germ cell tumors are usually cured if found and treated early.
source_span: Ovarian germ cell tumors are usually cured if found and treated early.

statement: There are four stages used for ovarian germ cell tumors: Stage I, Stage II, Stage III, and Stage IV.
source_span: Stage I     - Stage II     - Stage III     - Stage IV

statement: Staging of ovarian germ cell tumor typically involves a surgical procedure called a laparotomy to see if the cancer has spread.
source_span: an operation called a laparotomy is done to see if the cancer has spread

statement: Ovarian low malignant potential tumor is a disease in which abnormal cells form in the tissue covering the ovary.
source_span: abnormal cells form in the tissue covering the ovary

statement: Ovarian low malignant potential tumors have abnormal cells that may become cancer but usually do not, and the disease usually remains in the ovary.
source_span: Ovarian low malignant potential tumors have abnormal cells that may become cancer, but usually do not. This disease usually remains in the ovary.

statement: When disease is found in one ovary, the other ovary should also be checked carefully for signs of disease.
source_span: When disease is found in one ovary, the other ovary should also be checked carefully for signs of disease.

statement: The CA 125 assay measures the level of CA 125 in the blood, and an increased CA 125 level is sometimes a sign of cancer or other condition.
source_span: CA 125 assay : A test that measures the level of CA 125 in the blood...An increased CA 125 level is sometimes a sign of cancer or other condition.

statement: Prognosis and treatment options for ovarian low malignant potential tumor depend on the stage of the disease, the type of cells that make up the tumor, the size of the tumor, and the patient's general health.
source_span: The prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options depend on the following: - The stage of the disease...- What type of cells make up the tumor. - The size of the tumor. - The patients general health.

statement: Patients with ovarian low malignant potential tumors have a good prognosis, especially when the tumor is found early.
source_span: Patients with ovarian low malignant potential tumors have a good prognosis, especially when the tumor is found early.

statement: Most patients with ovarian low malignant potential tumor are diagnosed with stage I disease.
source_span: Most patients are diagnosed with stage I disease.

statement: Stage I of ovarian low malignant potential tumor is divided into stage IA, stage IB, and stage IC.
source_span: Stage I is divided into stage IA, stage IB, and stage IC.

statement: In stage IA, the tumor is found inside a single ovary.
source_span: Stage IA: The tumor is found inside a single ovary.

statement: In stage IB, the tumor is found inside both ovaries.
source_span: Stage IB: The tumor is found inside both ovaries.

statement: In stage IC, the tumor is found inside one or both ovaries and either tumor cells are found on the outside surface of one or both ovaries, or the ovary's capsule has ruptured, or tumor cells are found in peritoneal cavity fluid or peritoneal washings.
source_span: Stage IC: The tumor is found inside one or both ovaries and one of the following is true: - tumor cells are found on the outside surface of one or both ovaries; or - the capsule (outer covering) of the ovary has ruptured (broken open); or - tumor cells are found in the fluid of the peritoneal cavity...or in washings of the peritoneum

statement: Ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancers are diseases in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the ovaries, fallopian tubes, or peritoneum.
source_span: Ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancers are diseases in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the ovaries, fallopian tubes, or peritoneum.

statement: Ovarian cancer is the leading cause of death from cancer of the female reproductive system.

statement: Each ovary is about the size and shape of an almond.

statement: Primary peritoneal cancer is cancer that forms in the peritoneum and has not spread there from another part of the body.

statement: New cases of ovarian cancer and deaths from it are higher among white women than black women, but have decreased in both groups.

statement: Women with a family history of ovarian cancer and/or inherited gene changes such as BRCA1 or BRCA2 have a higher risk of ovarian cancer.
source_span: Women who have a family history of ovarian cancer and/or certain inherited gene changes, such as BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene changes, have a higher risk than women who do not have a family history

statement: A woman whose mother or sister had ovarian cancer has an increased risk of ovarian cancer.

statement: Estrogen-only hormone replacement therapy (HRT) after menopause is linked to a slightly increased risk of ovarian cancer in women taking it or who took it within the past 3 years.
source_span: The use of estrogen -only hormone replacement therapy (HRT) after menopause is linked to a slightly increased risk of ovarian cancer in women who are taking HRT or have taken HRT within the past 3 years.

statement: Being tall (5'8" or taller) may be linked to a slight increase in the risk of ovarian cancer.
source_span: Being tall (5'8" or taller) may also be linked to a slight increase in the risk of ovarian cancer.

statement: Taking oral contraceptives lowers the risk of ovarian cancer, and the decrease in risk may last up to 30 years after a woman stops taking them.
source_span: The decrease in risk may last up to 30 years after a woman has stopped taking oral contraceptives.

statement: Tubal ligation (surgery to close both fallopian tubes) decreases the risk of ovarian cancer.
source_span: The risk of ovarian cancer is decreased in women who have a tubal ligation (surgery to close both fallopian tubes).

statement: Taking oral contraceptives increases the risk of blood clots, and this risk is higher in women who also smoke.
source_span: Taking oral contraceptives increases the risk of blood clots. This risk is higher in women who also smoke.

statement: Gallbladder cancer is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the gallbladder.
source_span: Gallbladder cancer is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the gallbladder.

statement: The gallbladder is a pear-shaped organ that lies just under the liver in the upper abdomen.
source_span: The gallbladder is a pear-shaped organ that lies just under the liver in the upper abdomen.

statement: The wall of the gallbladder has 3 main layers of tissue: mucosal (inner), muscularis (middle, muscle), and serosal (outer).
source_span: The wall of the gallbladder has 3 main layers of tissue. - Mucosal (inner) layer. - Muscularis (middle, muscle) layer. - Serosal (outer) layer.

statement: Primary gallbladder cancer starts in the inner layer and spreads through the outer layers as it grows.
source_span: Primary gallbladder cancer starts in the inner layer and spreads through the outer layers as it grows.

statement: Patients with gallstones rarely develop gallbladder cancer.
source_span: Patients with gallstones rarely develop gallbladder cancer.

statement: Risk factors for gallbladder cancer include being female and being Native American.
source_span: Risk factors for gallbladder cancer include the following: - Being female. - Being Native American.

statement: Signs and symptoms of gallbladder cancer include jaundice, fever, and pain.
source_span: Signs and symptoms of gallbladder cancer include jaundice, fever, and pain.

statement: Other possible symptoms of gallbladder cancer include nausea and vomiting, bloating, and lumps in the abdomen.
source_span: Nausea and vomiting. - Bloating. - Lumps in the abdomen.

statement: The CA 19-9 assay measures the level of CA 19-9 in the blood, which when elevated can be a sign of gallbladder cancer or other conditions.
source_span: CA 19-9 is released into the bloodstream from both cancer cells and normal cells. When found in higher than normal amounts, it can be a sign of gallbladder cancer or other conditions.

statement: PTC (percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography) involves inserting a thin needle through the skin below the ribs into the liver to x-ray the liver and bile ducts.
source_span: A thin needle is inserted through the skin below the ribs and into the liver. Dye is injected into the liver or bile ducts and an x-ray is taken.

statement: Having had an undescended testicle is a risk factor for testicular cancer.
source_span: Having had an undescended testicle.

statement: Risk factors for testicular cancer also include abnormal development of the testicles, a personal history of testicular cancer, a family history of testicular cancer (especially in a father or brother), and being white.
source_span: Having had abnormal development of the testicles. - Having a personal history of testicular cancer. - Having a family history of testicular cancer (especially in a father or brother). - Being white.

statement: Certain treatments for testicular cancer can cause infertility that may be permanent.

statement: Patients who may wish to have children should consider sperm banking before having testicular cancer treatment.
source_span: Patients who may wish to have children should consider sperm banking before having treatment.

statement: The three tumor markers used in staging testicular cancer are alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH).

statement: Cancer can spread through three ways in the body: tissue, the lymph system, and the blood.
source_span: Cancer can spread through tissue, the lymph system, and the blood

statement: The stages used for testicular cancer are Stage 0 (Testicular Intraepithelial Neoplasia), Stage I, Stage II, and Stage III.
source_span: The following stages are used for testicular cancer: - Stage 0 (Testicular Intraepithelial Neoplasia) - Stage I - Stage II - Stage III

statement: In Stage 0 testicular cancer, abnormal cells are found in the tubules where sperm cells begin to develop, and all tumor marker levels are normal.

statement: Stage I testicular cancer is divided into stage IA, stage IB, and stage IS, and is determined after an inguinal orchiectomy is done.

statement: Tumor marker levels are measured again after inguinal orchiectomy and biopsy in order to determine the stage of testicular cancer.

statement: An ovarian cyst larger than 6 centimeters is a risk factor that increases the chance a hydatidiform mole will become cancer.
